query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases? Earlier studies of refractory and transition-metal-based high-entropy alloys primarily examined elemental and compositional effects involving Al, Cr, Si, Ti, and V, but the reported outcomes depended on composition limits, phase readjustment, and processing. This emphasis has not resolved the oxidation behavior of compositionally complex alloys, for which synergistic elemental effects make interpretation difficult. The starting alloy was designed to retain an fcc matrix for formability and has demonstrated notable strength and fatigue performance, so any explanation should account for its integrity without compromising those constraints. Define a controlled comparison that would distinguish the proposed explanation, predict observations relative to the starting-state baseline, identify applicable exposure boundaries and supporting prior evidence, and state an outcome that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: The degradation under elevated-temperature exposure in the Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 fcc high-entropy alloy is governed by a competition between the formation of a protective, multi‐layered oxide scale and internal degradation due to element segregation and sub‐surface phase reactions. Under oxidizing conditions, synergistic interactions among Cr, Ti, and minor Al promote the rapid formation of a thin, adherent oxide scale that protects the underlying fcc matrix, whereas under reducing conditions the suppression of protective scale formation leads to detrimental internal oxidation and phase boundary degradation.
generation.material_initial_state: As‐printed additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with a stable fcc matrix and minimal pre-existing precipitates or internal oxidation.
generation.intervention: Subject the alloy to controlled high-temperature exposure (700–900 °C) while systematically varying the gas environment by adjusting the O2:H2 ratio (from strongly oxidizing to mildly reducing) and exposing samples for durations up to 100 hours. A homogenized (annealed) version should be compared with the as-printed state.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperatures (700–900 °C) under well-controlled gas atmospheres with varying O2:H2 ratios and up to 100 h exposure durations.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and continuity of a multilayered oxide scale (including a Cr-rich and possibly an Al- or Ti-modified oxide sublayer) and the onset of sub-surface elemental segregation or phase transformations at matrix/oxide interfaces.
generation.mechanism: Synergistic elemental interactions in the alloy promote rapid oxide scale formation under oxidizing conditions that limits further oxygen ingress and preserves the fcc matrix integrity. When the gas environment is shifted toward reducing conditions, the driving force for protective scale formation is diminished, leading to enhanced internal degradation via elemental depletion and sub-surface reactions at phase boundaries.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under predominantly oxidizing gas atmospheres, samples will develop thin, continuous, and adherent oxide layers with minimal internal damage, thereby maintaining mechanical integrity. In contrast, under reducing conditions or at lower O2:H2 ratios, the oxide scale will be less protective (thicker, more porous or discontinuous) and increased internal oxidation or deleterious phase boundary reactions will be observable, signaling the onset of degradation.
generation.baseline: The as-printed alloy state showing a stable fcc matrix with initially limited oxide formation and no significant internal degradation prior to high-temperature gas exposure.
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 700–900 °C; Gas compositions: fully oxidizing (high O2 fraction) to mildly reducing (by increasing H2 content); Exposure duration: up to 100 hours.
generation.uncertainty: The precise gas ratio threshold at which the transition from protective scale formation to internal degradation occurs is uncertain, as is the quantitative contribution of each element (Cr, Ti, minor Al) to scale integrity. Variability due to processing history or microstructural heterogeneities may also influence outcomes.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 samples: one in the as-printed condition and one homogenized via annealing. Expose both sets in parallel at 700 °C, 800 °C, and 900 °C under a series of gas mixtures varying the O2:H2 ratio from fully oxidizing to reducing for durations up to 100 h. Post-exposure, perform cross-sectional microscopy (SEM/TEM) and microanalysis (EDS, XRD) to evaluate oxide scale thickness, continuity, composition, and sub-surface phase changes. Mechanical integrity tests (e.g., tensile or fatigue testing) should be conducted to assess the functional impact of any degradation.
measurements: Oxide scale thickness and morphology via SEM/TEM
Phase identification and composition of the oxide and sub-surface regions using EDS and XRD
Mechanical property measurements (e.g., tensile strength, fatigue resistance) pre- and post-exposure
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If varying the gas environment (O2:H2 ratio) does not result in a systematic transition between the formation of a protective thin, continuous oxide scale and internal degradation (e.g., no measurable difference in oxide scale quality, sub-surface phase changes, or mechanical performance between oxidizing and reducing conditions), then the proposed mechanism is falsified.

While the Base Alloy exhibited a mass gain of approximately 15 mg/cm2 after oxidation at 900 °C for 120 h, the addition of Cr2.5Co2.5Mn2.5 promoted the formation of a multilayered oxide scale (outer MnCr2O4/inner Al2O3), reducing the parabolic oxidation rate constant to 1.7 × 10−5 mg2·cm−4·s−1. The originality of this work lies in the coupling of compositional and microstructural engineering; further addition of 0.5 at.% Y decreased this constant to 1.7 × 10−6 mg2·cm−4·s−1—a three-order-of-magnitude reduction relative to the Base Alloy, while increasing the apparent oxidation activation energy to ~350 kJ/mol. decision.trend: Recent work on Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni–Ti alloys (PMC10095688) has focused on how heat treatment and precipitate evolution affect high-temperature mechanical performance in fcc-based compositions. Parallel studies of FeNiCuAl-based high-entropy alloys (PMC13208696) demonstrated that combined alloying elements facilitate a protective oxide scale in oxidizing atmospheres, but the precise role of each element and the transitions between protective oxide formation and internal degradation remain poorly understood. While these approaches reveal synergy among multiple elements at elevated temperature, neither fully resolves how concurrent oxidizing and reducing conditions influence sub-surface reactions and structural stability in fcc-based Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni–Ti alloys. The local, time-dependent oxidation mechanisms in the complex matrix remain unclarified, particularly regarding the competition between protective scale formation versus internal degradation paths.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear how the multi-element synergy in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni–Ti alloys dictates oxidation behavior when exposed to varying partial pressures of oxidizing versus reducing gases. In particular, the mechanistic drivers—whether protective oxide scale formation or internal reactions at phase boundaries dominate—are not fully established. The lack of a controlled study isolating the effect of gas composition and partial pressure on sub-surface chemistry and microstructure evolution leaves the oxidation mechanism incompletely understood.
decision.lever: Vary the gas environment (O2:H2 ratio), temperature (e.g., 700–900 °C), and exposure duration (e.g., up to 100 h) in a side-by-side comparison of the as-printed alloy versus a homogenized reference. Measure oxide scale composition, thickness, and sub-surface phase changes using cross-sectional microscopy and microanalysis.
decision.why: Implementing a series of carefully designed exposures, incrementally adjusting oxidizing-to-reducing ratios, isolates whether protective oxide layer formation or internal damage by alternative reaction pathways drives degradation in this Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni–Ti fcc alloy. Prior work (PMC13208696) shows that multi-element synergy can stabilize certain oxide scales, and (PMC10095688) highlights the critical role of microstructural evolution at elevated temperatures. Testing these variables in parallel under controlled environments would pinpoint the prevailing mechanism, clarify operating regimes, and enable direct falsification of mechanistic hypotheses if observed scale evolution and damage modes contradict the proposed controlling factors.
